en: The First Fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Great Secret King of All Tathāgatas,
the Unprecedented, Supreme, and Subtle Great Maṇḍala*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heavens, the Court-Scattered Grandee (Chao-san-dafu).

Translated by the Imperial Preceptor and Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Master Mingjiao, Tian Xizai, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Ritual Procedures for the Maṇḍala of Corresponding Practice. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the Great Hall of Good Dharma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, there were countless supreme devas and humans, as well as nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, mahābalas, apasmārakas, ḍākinīs, bhūtas, vetālas, and the mātṛkā-spirits; all of these, weary of saṃsāra and desiring to sever the cycle of rebirth, surrounded the World-Honored One seeking the Dharma of auspiciousness, and likewise joyfully sought the method for achieving the vast wisdom of the inexhaustible Vajradhātu.
At that time, there were also countless great bodhisattvas who, for the sake of benefiting the three realms, manifested signs of transformation through their pure wisdom. Their names were:

Bodhisattva Wisdom-Vajra, Bodhisattva Wisdom-Hook, Bodhisattva Wisdom-Desire, Bodhisattva Wisdom-Secret, Bodhisattva Consecration-Auspiciousness, Bodhisattva Great-Majestic-Power-Auspiciousness, Bodhisattva Banner-Auspiciousness, Bodhisattva Mindfulness-Auspiciousness, Bodhisattva Dharma-Sound, Bodhisattva Wisdom-Fury, Bodhisattva Cause-Fury, Bodhisattva Mouth-Fury, Bodhisattva Transformation-Action, Bodhisattva Transformation-Domain, Bodhisattva Transformation-Yakṣa, and Bodhisattva Transformation-Secrecy. All such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had fully realized the samādhi of the secret of dharma-wisdom.
Furthermore, there are four Family Mothers, whose names are:
Vajra Mother of the Samādhi of Perfect Wisdom, Vajra Mother of the Samādhi of Jewel Wisdom, Vajra Mother of the Samādhi of Dharma Wisdom, and Vajra Mother of the Samādhi of Karma Wisdom.
Furthermore, there were four Bodhisattvas of Great Supernatural Power, whose names were:
the Bodhisattva Vajrapakṣa-ṛddhi, the Bodhisattva Vajrasūkṣmapraveśa-ṛddhi, the Bodhisattva Vajrācalaprabha-ṛddhi, and the Bodhisattva Vajraprīti-ṛddhi.
Furthermore, there were eight great Bodhisattvas of secret transformation-manifestations who appeared to make offerings, named:

Vajrarati Bodhisattva, Vajrarūpa Bodhisattva, Vajrasvarā Bodhisattva, Vajraprīti Bodhisattva, Vajrasādhya Bodhisattva, Vajraphala Bodhisattva, Vajrottamavyūha Bodhisattva, and Vajragandhā Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there were sixteen powerful and sovereign yakṣas, great wrathful vidyārājas, and others, whose names were:
the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Aparājita-vīra, the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Aparājita,
the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Siddhikara, the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Parama-padma-prabha, and Hayamukha.
Mahākrodharāja, Padmāntakṛt Mahākrodharāja, Vighnāntaka Mahākrodharāja,
Amṛtakuṇḍalī Mahākrodharāja, Mahābala Mahākrodharāja, Tejorāśi Mahākrodharāja, and Hayagrīva Mahākrodharāja.
Rudhaka Mahākrodharāja, Ananta Mahākrodharāja, Vajrācala Mahākrodharāja,
Tara Mahākrodharāja, Cunda Mahākrodharāja, Sitātapatra Mahākrodharāja, and Uttaramati Mahākrodharāja.
The King is the Six-Faced Great Wrathful Vidyārāja.
Furthermore, there are the sixteen Great Female Form Vidyārājas and others, whose names are:

the Great Vidyārājñī Tārā, the Great Vidyārājñī Aparājitā, the Great Vidyārājñī Śrī-mahādevī (Peacock), the Great Vidyārājñī Vajrāṅkuśī, the Great Vidyārājñī Mahānāmā, the Great Vidyārājñī Bhṛkuṭī, the Great Vidyārājñī Māmakī, the Great Vidyārājñī Vajrasaṃkalā, the Great Vidyārājñī Vajramuṣṭi, the Great Vidyārājñī Sitātapatrā (White One), the Great Vidyārājñī Ratnaśikhā, the Great Vidyārājñī Vajragati, the Great Vidyārājñī Vajrakāyā, the Great Vidyārājñī Vajragandhā, and the Great Vidyārājñī Lokadhāriṇī.
Furthermore, there is the Great Vidyārājñī in female form who possesses four corresponding characteristics; furthermore, there are sixty-four great Vajra-Ḍākinīs.
Furthermore, there are four Earth Goddesses (Mahāpṛthivī-devīs), whose names are:
the Immovable Earth Goddess, the Yellow-Faced Earth Goddess, the Black-and-White Earth Goddess, and the Red-Faced Earth Goddess.
These and other such Mahāpṛthivī devas are able to accomplish all tasks, bestow all desires, and abide securely in all dharmas.
Furthermore, there are eight great Mārīcīs, whose names are:
Vajramukhī Mahāmārīcī, Pītamukhī Mahāmārīcī, Virūpamukhī Mahāmārīcī, Raktakāyā Mahāmārīcī, Bahumukhī Mahāmārīcī, Triśikhā Mahāmārīcī, Rudhirāśanā Mahāmārīcī, and Rakta-pītā Mahāmārīcī.
Such great malarial spirits as these constantly afflict sentient beings, causing them to lose their physical strength and beauty, or even taking their lives.

All such deities and their lords, the vidyādharas and their lords, as well as the nāgas and their lords, the gandharvas and their lords, the kiṃnaras and their lords—even all those with evil minds or extremely evil minds, and those who are good or extremely good—all such multitudes have gathered here.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having surveyed this assembly of the great multitude, entered the Samādhi of the Adornment of the Vairocana All-Vajra Maṇḍala; he then emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows, from his heart, and from his navel, illuminating all worlds.
When that light had illuminated all worlds, it returned once more and entered the heart of the Vajra-correspondence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, having adjusted his robes and composed his countenance amidst the great assembly, rose from his seat. He cast a vajra into the presence of the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and offered a profound salutation. Having completed his obeisance, he joined his palms and spoke these words of praise:

“I now take refuge in Vairocana, the supreme and fearless one, who can expound the great dhāraṇī of empowerment for the accomplishment of subjugation. He desires to cause sentient beings to awaken to the markless wisdom of neither arising nor ceasing, and is able to shatter the great terrors of saṃsāric birth and death.”
Having thus praised himself, he addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
I now have a doubt that I wish to inquire about; I pray that you will grant me your pity and explain it for me."
"Bhagavān! When a Vajrācārya constructs a maṇḍala, how should he select the site?
How many kinds of sites are there?"
How does one perform the rite of purification?
How does one drive in the ritual stakes?
And how can one destroy all evil obstacles and difficulties?
How does one release the fetters of all signs?
How are even the nāgas to be subdued?
Furthermore, regarding the performance of recitation, how is the homa ritual to be conducted?
Furthermore, how should the ritual of fire be performed?
Moreover, how many kinds of maṇḍalas should there be,
and how many gates should be opened?
How many kinds of gates are there,
and what are their characteristics?
Furthermore, what is the significance of the outer maṇḍala?
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the inner maṇḍala?
What is the significance of the wheel-sign in its center?
How should the boundaries of the maṇḍala be delineated?
How are the lines to be drawn?
What are the dimensions of the bodies of the deity to be visualized and those of the noble ones?
And how high should the pavilion and the precious throne be?
As for the mudrās, what are their characteristics?
Furthermore, how should a powdered maṇḍala be constructed?
How many kinds of powder are there?
What is the sequence for the successive stages of scattering the powder?
Furthermore, what are the rules for the *ācārya*’s reception of disciples?
Regarding the disciple’s practice, what dharma should be cultivated first?
Furthermore, what are the rules for the preliminary practices (*pūrvasevā*) performed by one who maintains the recitation?
Moreover, what is the sequence for a disciple’s entry into the maṇḍala?
And how are the various vidyās and mudrās of the chosen deity to be transmitted and received?
How many types of rituals for the offering of food and its generation are there?
What items should be offered to the Ācārya?
Furthermore, what should be the dimensions of the various auspicious vases (kalaśas) offered to the Buddhas and Tathāgatas?
How should the neck and mouth of the flask be fashioned?
Furthermore, how is the rite of empowerment (abhiṣeka) performed?
According to the ritual, what should be used for each purpose?
Furthermore, what is meant by the "Secret Maṇḍala"?

World-Honored One, I now inquire about each of these matters one by one, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; I only pray that, out of your compassion, you will explain them extensively for me.
Having spoken these words, he returned to his original seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Vajrapāṇi, since you have attained great fearlessness and are endowed with great compassion, you are able to pose this question before me; listen attentively, for I shall explain it to you."
Then Vajrapāṇi looked up at the Buddha with focused attention and remained there, receiving the instruction.
The Buddha said: “Vajrapāṇi!”
The elements of the earth are vast and each possesses its own characteristics; to speak of them in general terms, there are four kinds, which are distinguished according to the four castes.
These four castes are: the Kṣatriya, the Brāhmaṇa, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
These constitute the four.
Regarding the method for selecting the site, there are likewise four types according to its fragrance, flavor, or color:
first, those of the Kṣatriya caste seek land that is red in color;
Second, those of the Brahmin caste seek white ground;
third, those of the Vaiśya seek deep yellow ground;
fourth, those of the Śūdra seek black ground.
Furthermore, one discerns the ground by its fragrance:
the ground of a kṣatriya is imbued with the scent of various lotuses;
the ground of a brāhmaṇa has the scent of blue lotuses.
The scent of the Vaiśya stage is the fragrance of women's touch;
the scent of the Śūdra stage is the fragrance of orpiment.
Furthermore, they are distinguished by their tastes:
The ground of the kṣatriyas has a taste like iron, yet it also possesses a sweet flavor;
the ground of the brāhmaṇas is pungent and bitter;
the ground of the vaiśyas has a flavor that is exclusively sweet.
The ground of Śūdra is bitter and pungent in taste.
On such ground, one should focus the mind with single-minded concentration to discern and select it.
Having obtained this ground, one should establish the boundary by driving in stakes.
Regarding the method for fashioning the ritual stakes (*kīla*), there are likewise four types according to the *maṇḍala* rites:
if for the purpose of pacifying (*śāntika*), use wood containing sap to make the stake;
if for the purpose of increasing (*pauṣṭika*), use auspicious wood or *śrīśa* wood to make the stake.
If for the purpose of subjugation, use stakes made of khadira wood;
if for the purpose of subduing, use stakes made of iron.
Furthermore, if following the mantra of the Wrathful King Cundā, use stakes according to the rite for pacification (śāntika).
If one employs the mantra of the Supreme Vidyārāja Padma, one should use a kīla for the rite of augmentation (puṣṭi);
if one follows the mantra of a Mahābala Vidyārāja, one should use a kīla for the rites of subjugation (abhicāra) and subduing (vaśīkaraṇa).
Furthermore, if one wishes to dispel all evils, terrors, obstacles, and difficulties, one should employ the Universal Radiance Mudrā, the Hammer Mudrā, and their respective mantras;
if one wishes to bind and restrain those who are extremely wicked, one should employ the Vajrakarma and Vajrapāśa Mudrās, mantras, and so forth.
This mudrā and mantra must not be employed recklessly unless directed against those who are extremely wicked;
if this rite is performed against an extremely wicked person, one must subsequently release them;
and after releasing them, one must still offer them food as a sacrificial gift for their sustenance.

Furthermore, when performing rites at the three types of fire altars (*agnikuṇḍa*), or when a disciple performs the preliminary practices (*pūrvasevā*), or when performing the *maṇḍala* homa, one should employ the mantras and vidyās for increasing all accomplishments, along with incense, flowers, and other offerings, as a sacrificial rite for the purpose of subduing and binding all obstructors and difficulties.
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! There are four types of gates for constructing a maṇḍala.”
"Those which face east, south, west, and north constitute the four types. Vajrapāṇi asked,
"What karmic fruit is obtained by one who enters through its gates?"
The Buddha said: “Vajrapāṇi!
A maṇḍala has an outer, an inner, and a middle section. One who constructs a maṇḍala should divide it into nine parts; these nine parts constitute the supreme maṇḍala.”
The four gates are now clearly distinguished; the results sought through the practices performed at each of these four gates differ.

If one seeks to become a sovereign of the great earth, to achieve the accomplishment of the sword, to enter the palace of the asuras, or to attain peace, happiness, and the wisdom of liberation, one should perform recitation and ritual practice at the eastern gate.

If one seeks the accomplishment of sacred medicines, abundant wealth and grain, or even peace, auspiciousness, and the pacification of all calamities and misfortunes, one should perform recitation and ritual practice at the southern gate.

If one seeks to be loved and respected by all people, to ensure the prosperity of one's descendants, the abundance of wealth and grain, or to pacify calamities and attain peace and happiness, one may perform the recitation ritual at the western gate.

If one seeks to subjugate enemies, to tame all who are extremely wicked, or to perform heroic deeds and provide protection for the practitioner, one may perform the recitation ritual at the northern gate.
"Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!
If one practices the yoga according to the mantravidhi, then according to one's own faith and inclination, one will be able to achieve accomplishment through each respective gateway."

"If there are those who, with faith and joy, cultivate the ritual procedures of yoga, focusing one-pointedly on investigating the words and meanings to seek the dharma of non-self, they shall enter through the eastern gate."
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bhagavān, saying:
"What should the outer maṇḍala be called?
The Buddha replied:
"Vajrapāṇi! Regarding the name of the outer maṇḍala: just as within a great temple there are halls and towers that must necessarily be protected by outer walls, so too it is with the outer maṇḍala."
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! Furthermore, just as the fruit of wisdom can only be accomplished through diligent protection, so too it is with the outer maṇḍala.”
Furthermore, just as a seed is enclosed within its husk, with the husk on the outside and the seed within, so too is it with the inner maṇḍala.

Moreover, one should place the seed-wheel at the center; the wheel-sign manifests the meaning of reality, or the letter *ka* may be placed to signify the meaning of karma (*karma*), and the letter *ra* to signify the meaning of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The internal and external have already been explained; what, then, is the middle?”
The Buddha said:
"Divide the maṇḍala exactly into three parts: one part is the outer, one part is the inner, and one part is the middle.
Vajrapāṇi addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"How should one draw the lines for constructing the maṇḍala?
The Buddha said:
"Construct it by drawing the lines according to the superior, middling, and inferior [levels]."
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! First, through the samādhi of the union of wisdom and skillful means, one should visualize oneself transforming into the Tathāgata.”

Once this visualization is accomplished, one subsequently employs the seal of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*) and so forth to draw forth the Tathāgata’s vajra-wind from space, causing the vajra-wind to pervade the entire earth element.
Furthermore, one visualizes upon that wind-circle ground the seal of the Vajra-vidyārāja "A" syllable;
and furthermore, one contemplates upon the four-jeweled vajra mountain the "Hūṃ" syllable, known as the Supreme Great Vajra Jewel Peak of Universal Manifestation.

Above it is a great jeweled palace, adorned with various ornaments such as vajra-jewel pillars, jewel bells, jewel robes, banners, pennants, and necklaces; within that palace dwells the Tathāgata Lotus-Jewel-Colored, and this is called the Samādhi Maṇḍala.

Having performed this visualization and understood each detail thoroughly, one again freely performs the four vajra steps, binds the mudrā of the Great Malevolent Wrathful Vidyārāja, and recites the mantra, making the vajra-fist gesture and performing fearless steps like a dance.
Having performed such contemplation, one should then adorn the maṇḍala with the seal-mantras and place the symbols within it, offering incense, flowers, and so forth. "Vajrapāṇi!

If there are practitioners who can thus give rise to this resolve without failing in even a single instance, they are indeed those who practice the teachings of the Tathāgata’s mantras; I shall therefore bestow upon them the empowerment through the empowerment rite by means of my own majestic power.

If that practitioner, for the sake of all sentient beings, seeks to dedicate [merit] toward the fruit of unsurpassed wisdom during the three periods of the day, they should perform the appropriate visualization and contemplate all sentient beings as the deity; in this manner, they should understand each and every one of them clearly.

Furthermore, the Vajrācārya, as well as those who practice together and even the disciples, must likewise understand this; only then should they empower the ground, establish the boundary, and create the vajra-ground.

Having further completed the praise with auspicious and wondrous sounds, one first makes offerings in the northwest direction with the adamantine supreme vidyā-mantra while directing the mind with sincere resolve;
next, one makes offerings in the northeast direction using the adamantine staff;
and next, one makes offerings in the southeast direction using the adamantine fire.
Next, in the southwest, one should perform the offering with a vajra-sword.

Having thus completed the offerings, the ācārya then leads the disciple, having him hold the cord, and proceeds from the northwest to mark out the measurements, then to the northeast, then to the southeast, and then to the southwest.

Having thus completed the planning, measurement, and determination, one then begins from the northwest and proceeds clockwise to stretch lines and establish the boundary paths, forming a square shape divided into three layers: inner, outer, and middle.

Having thus completed the visualization, one should request the Vajrācārya to perform various offerings; then, in the northwest direction, to the left of the reciter, one first forms the tortoise mudrā and places it upon the ground.
However, the Ācārya begins from the northwest, touches his right knee to the ground, and lowers the powder with his right hand.
First he lowers white powder, then red, then yellow, then green, and finally black powder.

From this point forward, the sequence for applying the powder shall always be followed as a standard procedure. The applied powder must not cover or obstruct the boundary lines; furthermore, the powder applied must not be uneven in thickness or coarse and fine, nor should it be crooked or distorted. Wherever there are pre-existing gaps in the applied powder, they must be filled in to restore completeness.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bhagavān, saying:
"What do the five colors of the powder signify?
What further meaning do they possess?"
The Buddha said:
“It is like an old garment that is originally white; if one wishes to dye it with a pleasing color, one must first wash it with water to make it clean.
Once it has been washed clean and its whiteness is pure, it can then be dyed into the desired pleasing color.”

One should cause the reciter and his disciples to first purify the stains of their prior negative karma with the water of the maṇḍala rite; thereafter, they shall be dyed with the colors of profound wisdom and meaning to achieve the desired hue.
The four colors—white, red, yellow, and green—of these powders can extinguish the transgressions committed against the Great Brahma-conduct.
Black signifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva Māmakī. In the center of the inner maṇḍala, one should draw a wheel design using exclusively the color white.
On all the gates and four corners of the outer maṇḍala, one should place *argha* vases, which should be filled with the five jewels, the five medicines, the five grains, and so forth.
Vajrapāṇi asked: "How many kinds of argha-vases are there,
and what are their dimensions?"
The Buddha said:
"Vajrapāṇi! There should be seven kinds of argha-vases, namely:
Gold vessels, silver vessels, copper vessels, glass vessels, iron vessels, wooden vessels, and earthenware vessels—
such as these are the seven kinds of vessels.
Vajrapāṇi! For rites of pacification, increase, and empowerment, one may use a golden flask, a crystal flask, or an earthenware flask;
for rites of subjugation, subduing, and the practice of asuras, one may use a copper flask.
If one performs various wrathful rites (*krodha-vidhi*), silver, iron, wood, or similar materials may be used.
Furthermore, O Vajrapāṇi!

That *argha* vase should be twenty finger-widths (*aṅgula*) in height, sixteen finger-widths in the width of its belly, five finger-widths in the height of its neck, and eight finger-widths in the breadth of its mouth; these proportions constitute the most excellent.
The maṇḍala should employ the colors of those vases;
for the rite of pacification (śāntika), use white vases;
for the rite of enrichment (pauṣṭika), use yellow vases.
If for the rite of attraction and love, use a red-colored flask;
if for the rite of subjugation, use an extremely black-colored flask.
The silk cloth used to tie all the flasks should correspond to the color of each respective flask.
"Furthermore, as for the vase of the subjugation rite, its neck is slender and curved; this is indeed auspicious.
Vajrapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does one perform the empowerment rite for a disciple?"
"What is the measurement of the initiation maṇḍala?
The Buddha said, "Vajrapāṇi!"

First, to the northwest of the great maṇḍala, one should draw the initiation maṇḍala according to the dimensions of the inner maṇḍala. In its center, one should draw a boundary consisting of either three or seven layers, with gates drawn on each of the four sides. Within each gate, one should draw the guardian deity of that respective direction; likewise, one should also draw the guardian deities of their respective positions in the four intermediate corners and at the zenith and nadir. These should be depicted in the manner of descending from heaven, each holding celestial flowers, exquisite garlands, and so forth.
Furthermore, take four *argha* vases; having first consecrated each one with mantras, place them at the four corners.
Then, in the center of the maṇḍala, draw a lion throne. Once it is finished, perform offerings using incense produced from milky trees, various flowers, and even exquisite foods.
"Whoever receives initiation within this maṇḍala shall have all their present transgressions, whether light or heavy, completely extinguished.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi asked:
"What are the dimensions and colors of the various noble deities within the maṇḍala?"
"Furthermore, what is the height and depth of those seats? The Buddha said, "Vajrapāṇi!"
There are four types of maṇḍala deities: namely, those represented by symbols (cihna), or cast, or painted, or carved from wood.

Their dimensions should correspond to the gates of the maṇḍala; whatever is fashioned should be made complete, fully endowed with dharma-mudrās and adorned with circular halos, so that the deity thus created is rendered exceptionally sublime.
Furthermore, place Akṣobhya Buddha in the east, his body light blue;
place Ratnasambhava Buddha in the south, his body light yellow;
and place Amitāyus Buddha in the west, his body pure red.
In the north resides Amoghasiddhi Buddha, his body the color of a great green jewel.

Each of these Tathāgatas sits upon a precious throne corresponding to their respective direction; from the various ornaments of their crowns and topknots, there is nothing that does not fully accord with the adornments of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, in the center, one constructs the path of the three realms; using pure white, one forms the heart-wheel (*citta-cakra*), within which one draws the seal (*mudrā*) of Vairocana;
likewise, Akṣobhya Tathāgata performs the earth-touching seal (*bhūmisparśa-mudrā*), and Ratnasambhava Tathāgata performs the boon-granting seal (*varada-mudrā*).
The Tathāgata Amitāyus performs the mudrā of meditative concentration;
the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi performs the mudrā of granting fearlessness.
These mudrās are to be employed together with their respective mantras.
Furthermore, outside the Vajra Maṇḍala, the noble deities of the pavilions shall each have their own separate maṇḍala, ten feet in width and fully adorned.

The seats for these noble deities are slightly lower than the seat of the Buddha; they are arranged according to the noble deities of their respective families, as well as the seats for the Mothers of those families, the World Protectors, and the various celestial lords, with heights corresponding to the maṇḍala.
Additionally, the seats for the King of the Yāma Heaven and his celestial noble deities are four finger-widths high.
"Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!
Having thus constructed the maṇḍala, the ācārya must with a sincere mind offer flower garlands, necklaces, vajra bells, and whisks, as well as exquisite incense, arghya water, and so forth."
One should properly prepare eight or sixteen *argha* vases, all of which must be filled with scented water according to the ritual rules.
Furthermore, it is most excellent to light lamps using high-quality ghee.
If one is performing rites for accomplishment, one should light the lamp with white mustard seed oil;
if for rites of middling or inferior efficacy, one may use ordinary oil to light the lamp.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi asked:
"Regarding those who make offerings with flowers, how many varieties are there according to their respective rites?
Likewise, regarding substances such as unguents and incense, how many varieties are there that are auspicious or inauspicious?"
The Buddha said:

"The *mālikā* flower, the *aśoka* flower, the *makula* flower, the *jāti* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *yūthikā* flower, the *kumuda* flower, the *nirmālikā* flower, the *tagara* flower, and the *kārpūra* flower—these various flowers are all auspicious and may be used for offerings throughout the three families (*trikulāni*).
Furthermore, the *campaka* flower, the *aśoka* flower, and the *puṇḍarīka* flower—such flowers as these may be offered to the supreme maṇḍala."

Furthermore, with *kūṭaja* flowers, *siddhika* flowers, golden flowers, *śirīṣa* flowers, *kaṇikāra* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *utpala* flowers—such flowers as these should constantly be used to make offerings to the Great Lotus Family (*mahāpadmakula*).

Moreover, with *utpala* flowers, *tagara* flowers, *kuñcita* flowers, *karaṇḍaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, white lotuses, and various other lotuses, as well as flowers of exquisite fragrance, flowers of wondrous liberation, *damana* flowers, and *sumanā* flowers—such flowers as these may be used to make offerings to the Secret Maṇḍala.
The various flowers mentioned above are all auspicious flowers and may be offered according to the ritual rules.
Furthermore, as for *akula* flowers and *karavīra* flowers, the Buddha did not permit their use because they are inauspicious.

Additionally, regarding other flowers that are neither foul-smelling nor thorny, and which have not been damaged or plucked by anyone, one may make offerings of them according to one's means and capacity.
This constitutes the middling [grade], suitable for the offering of the *dhāraṇī* maṇḍala and the *krodha* (wrathful) maṇḍala.
Furthermore, regarding the various types of incense and so forth, there are also distinctions in their ritual application for making offerings.
They are as follows:
white sandalwood, musk, dūruṣka incense, olibanum, uśīra incense, śrīvāsaka incense, māṃsī incense, musta incense, and ghusṛṇa incense.

Thus, these various fragrances are pounded and sifted into powder and mixed with granulated sugar; this constitutes blended incense (*saṃyuktagandha*), which may be used for making offerings to the supreme maṇḍala.
Furthermore, white sandalwood, camphor, aloeswood, musk, and undecayed *kunkuma*—incenses such as these may be used for making offerings to the intermediate maṇḍala.

Moreover, using *guggulu* resin, ox horn, camel hair, and the skin of a mongoose, these are ground into fine particles and mixed with the sap of *mānī* wood to form incense; such incenses are to be used for the rites of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Furthermore, red sandalwood, black medicinal substances, black wool, and pungent aromatics—such fragrances as these may be used in the *vaśīkaraṇa* maṇḍala.
If one obtains various exquisite fragrances according to one's means and capacity, they may be used for making offerings in the dhāraṇī maṇḍala, the supreme wrathful (*krodha*) maṇḍala, and so forth.
Furthermore, one should offer various kinds of food and drink to the noble deities of the maṇḍala, namely:
ghee, milk, honey-curd, and various beverages; as well as cakes, sugar-cakes, oil-cakes, sweetmeats, milk-gruel, and various vegetables, all presented as offerings.
Furthermore, when making food offerings, one should use various vessels, namely:
vessels of gold, silver, copper, or earthenware; or else leaves from trees, lotus leaves, or leaves from the *bhallātaka* tree.
Regarding the aforementioned vessels and leaves, those that have not yet been touched are the most pure and thus the most supreme.

Furthermore, for the offerings generated from the *śāntika* (pacifying) and *pauṣṭika* (augmenting) maṇḍalas, as well as for the ācārya’s own consumption, the three white foods alone are the most supreme.
The "three white" items are:
milk, curd, and rice (or cooked rice).
Alternatively, other foods that are white in color may also be used.
For offering to the various deities of the Maṇḍala of Peaceful and Other [Deities], one should add sweet flavors; the food vessels should be made of copper or leaves.
For a Maṇḍala for subjugation and other such rites, pungent and bitter flavors should further be added.
The food consumed by that ācārya shall not exceed the three white foods.

Furthermore, for each and every maṇḍala, there must be external offerings consisting of banners and streamers, necklaces, exquisite incense, flower garlands, unguents, burning incense, lamps and candles, and arghya water.

Furthermore, the ācārya thoroughly understands each of the ritual procedures corresponding to the aforementioned maṇḍalas; he is able to comprehend the profound principles of the mantras and mudrās of the tutelary deity; moreover, donning the armor of diligence and wielding fierce weapons, he rides the chariot of non-retrogression and steadfastly cultivates the three secrets. Possessing great power within the triple world, he receives the supreme offerings of humans and devas.

In this way, the ācārya constantly cultivates meditative equipoise (samādhi) and, for the sake of his disciples, performs empowerments (abhiṣeka), homa rites, or constructs maṇḍalas to bring them benefit.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi said:
"In performing fire-offering rites (*homa*) such as those for pacifying or increasing merit, how should the hearth be constructed?
What are the mudrās?"
The Buddha said: “Vajrapāṇi!
Regarding the various homa hearths, if explained in detail, there are five hundred kinds; however, according to the present method of exposition, there are briefly four types.”
First, the fire-pit for pacifying; second, the fire-pit for increasing; third, the fire-pit for magnetizing; and fourth, the fire-pit for subjugating.
Even all methods of accomplishment (*siddhi*) and methods of subduing do not depart from these four types of rites.
First, the fire pit for pacifying (śāntika) is circular, resembling the form of a lotus;
second, the fire pit for increasing (pauṣṭika) is square, with its length and breadth being equal;
third, it is triangular.
The fourth is like a half-moon.
For each mantra and mudrā, follow its respective ritual procedure. "Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!"
The fire pit for pacifying (śāntika) is white in color, with its rim shaped like a lotus;
the fire pit for increasing (pauṣṭika) is golden in color, with a vajra-shaped rim;
the fire pit for subjugating (abhicāruka) is dark red or the color of flames.
Regarding the *kāmāgni* hearth, it is shaped like a half-moon and is exclusively red in color.
Each *homa* hearth has its own respective mudrā:
for the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one uses the lotus mudrā.
For the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), use the hook mudrā;
for the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), use the root mudrā.

As described above, place these various mudrās within the *homa* hearth. The *homa* hearth shall be one cubit (*hasta*) in height and twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in depth; its base shall be one cubit wide with a width of one fist-finger-breadth. In the center, construct a small platform eight finger-breadths in length and breadth and two finger-breadths in height, upon which the mudrā is to be placed.

For the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), the altar for the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*) is four finger-widths high and twelve finger-widths in length and breadth. In its center, one forms a lotus symbol two finger-widths high; upon this lotus sits the Fire Deity. The body of the Fire Deity is the color of milk, with a full topknot and adorned with a crown. His two hands form the mudrā of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*), and he wears white robes. From his eyes issue rays of light and the syllable *Jvala*, which enter into the fire and sit upon the lotus. The flames are blazing and intense, possessing hundreds of thousands of layers.
"Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!
One should construct a homa fire-pit for the preliminary rites, adorning the pit with powders of five colors and embellishing it with five lotus flowers."
On the four sides surrounding the exterior of the hearth, install the mudrās of the respective directional deities or the mantras of the wrathful vidyārājas.
The mantra of the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja is: Oṃ nuṣṭha vajra krodha hana hana hūṃ phaṭ. The Great Wrathful Mudrā:
"Press the left hand against the heart, extend three fingers, and join the thumb with the little finger; do the same with the right hand, crossing them before the heart like a vajra."
This mudrā serves as the supreme preparatory rite (*pūrvasevā*).
Alternatively, it may be used to dispel all fetters; perform this mudrā with the right hand as previously described, employing it in conjunction with the Jvara-mantra.
The mantra for entering the bonds is:

Oṃ jvala hūṃ phaṭ. Furthermore, when the practitioner performing the recitation performs the *karmahoma* and invokes the fire deity, they may use *bodhi* wood, *udumbara* wood, *nyagrodha* wood, or wood from trees with abundant sap as fuel; it must be moist and not dry, and the fire should be lit to perform the invocation ritual.
The Seal for Summoning the Fire Deity:
With the right hand held flat and facing upward, bend the thumb into the palm and bend the second joint of the index finger to form the seal.
The Mantra for Summoning the Fire Deity:
"Oṃ agnaye hihīhe śāntiṃ me kuru hutaśanāya svāhā. With this mudrā and mantra, invite the Fire Deity (Agnideva) to enter the lotus within the fire before you.

The practitioner of recitation visualizes the Fire Deity (Agni), whose body is the color of snow; his right hand holds a rosary and his left hand holds a pure flask. He displays an expression of compassion, has three eyes on his face, and his head is adorned with a jeweled crown and a topknot, fully endowed with all ornaments.

If one of another lineage performs this for the sake of a maṇḍala, all accomplishments will be attained. One should place the heart-mantras of each respective lineage within the lotuses; in the lotus at the rear edge, place the seal of the Supreme Vidyārāja of the White Elephant;
in the lotus on the right, place the vajra-mallet; and on the left, place a lotus the color of milk.
These are used identically for the homa in all instances. Furthermore, one should offer arghya water, incense, flowers, and so forth to the Fire God.
"The Ritual for the Vajra Mother Bhikṣuṇī:
The Ācārya holds the homa ladle and performs the homa with it full. The Homamantra:"
“Oṃ hūṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa gṛhṇāpaya siddhiṃ me prayaccha svāhā. The Vajramātā Sruvagrahaṇamudrā: Holding a ladle with the right hand, form a fist with the index finger and press it upon the hearth;
then, with both hands, form the jewel-binding (*ratnabandha*) gesture, crossing the two little fingers, while the remaining fingers are arranged like the *karmavajra* mudrā.
Having formed this mudrā and recited the aforementioned mantra, fill the ladle and perform the homa offering to the Fire Deity; then, dismiss [the deity] and move it to one side within the hearth.

"Furthermore, perform the homa: first, as the preliminary rite, recollect the name of the deity according to the specific ritual; then, with a sincere mind, make offerings and perform the homa by making three oblations with the full ladle according to the ritual rules. Furthermore, offer the mantras and mudrās of the vajra-mallet and other implements."

Having performed these preliminaries, one should then carry out the primary objective—whether for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*) or increase (*puṣṭi*)—by constructing a maṇḍala and performing various rites to make offerings to the noble deities.
Once their wishes have been fulfilled, he shall then dismiss and invite all the worthy sages to each return to their original positions.

Chapter Two: The Chapter on Empowerment (Abhiṣeka). At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I myself know that my excellent merit is perfected, and I have now attained the meaning of the subtle maṇḍala.
Furthermore, who else might be taken in and accepted as a disciple?”
Furthermore, in which country should the disciples be born so that they may be received and guided?
Among the four great castes—
the Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, and Śūdra— which caste is superior among these four for the purpose of being received and guided?
The Buddha said: “Vajrapāṇi!

Amitābha Buddha and Vairocana Buddha are the great ācāryas who are the masters of the secret Dharma within the triple world. They are without marks and without intrinsic nature, neither arising nor ceasing; though they abide in the secret, they possess no characteristic of secrecy. Future ācāryas must likewise understand this with clarity.”
Once this has been fully understood, one abides in the samādhi of the Vajra Lotus Lord, who possesses great compassion and great power. "Vajrapāṇi!
I shall now declare the countries and regions where those disciples will be born.

Whether they belong to the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa castes, those born in Śrāvastī, Magadha, China, Samataṭa, Kānyakubja, Rada, Nepāla, Jūniya, Anarta, Kośala, Kauṅkaṇa, Mālava, or Narmadā—those born in such lands as these may all be received and guided.
Furthermore, if there are none from the aforementioned central lands, those born in Siṃhala or any other country may likewise be received and guided.
Furthermore, the people of the country of Kīra are also included among those who receive [the Buddha’s] guidance, for a most supreme Muni was once born in that land.

In the aforementioned countries, if those of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa castes are born there, and if they rely upon an ācārya to receive and practice the teachings as practitioners, they will certainly attain perfection.

Furthermore, the ācārya should have a countenance that is serene, upright, and perfect; he should possess a heart of compassion and a pure mind, being sincere and free from deceit. He must have subdued his sensory faculties, having little greed and few desires. Endowed with great eloquence and profound wisdom, his speech is gentle and clear. By nature, he is not stingy but delights in giving; he is without envy or fear, has distanced himself from pride, and always rejoices in making offerings to the Great Ācāryas and the assembly of worthy sages.

Furthermore, he is able to expound the Dharma of *tathatā* (suchness), constantly practicing the conduct of mantras, refraining from praising his own virtues while always extolling the merits of others. All his accomplishments (*siddhi*) and all that he cultivates reach complete perfection; he neither finds fault with nor disparages his disciples, nor does he harbor any expectations regarding them. With a heart of great compassion, he addresses the worthy sages and noble ones, causing his disciples to enter all maṇḍalas by relying on the corresponding practices.

He further causes the disciples to attain liberation by relying on the ritual procedures (*vidhi*), ensuring that cause and effect correspond, and transmits to the disciples the Dharma of suchness through mantras and mudrās.
The disciple said:
"O Ācārya! How can this Dharma of the mantra, mudrā, and *tathatā* (suchness) be attained?"
The Ācārya said: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of the Buddha, listen attentively!"

The Buddha taught that this mantra flows forth from the wisdom of the perfection of *tathatā* through skillful means; it manifests as a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha within the triple world, displaying the power of diligence to provide exhortation, instruction, and guidance. Its meaning is profoundly excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; by means of this samādhi, one relies upon the practice of the Vajra-Lotus to teach Vajrasattva and others.

I, the Śākya clan, acting as a venerable ācārya out of compassion for all sentient beings, have now attained one hundred or three hundred mantra-dhāraṇīs within this clan. According to one’s own preference, through the power of accordance with *tathatā*, these may be written down and transmitted to disciples; by upholding, reciting, and practicing them, one shall bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings so that they never cease.

Once the disciple has received the instructions transmitted by the ācārya, he should prostrate at the feet of the ācārya and, with a devout mind, offer gold, silver, precious gems, elephants, horses, and even his own person to the ācārya and the noble deities of the maṇḍala.
Then the ācārya utters the words of the vajrasattva-samādhi:
"Child, receive this secret dharma.
Then the ācārya recites the *dhāraṇī* for the sake of bearing witness, and at that time, the assembly of vidyās provides this testimony:

"Now, [Name], in accordance with the Dharma, I offer this gold, silver, precious gems, as well as elephants, horses, and so forth, for the sake of seeking [a specific] objective and as an offering to the maṇḍala."

Then, the ācārya separately constructs the initiation maṇḍala and has the disciple sit cross-legged upon a lion throne within the maṇḍala. The disciple himself forms the vajra-joined-palms mudrā and remains with it placed at his heart.

Then the ācārya again empowers the first argha-vase with the mantra of the principal deity (iṣṭadevatā) and places it within the maṇḍala. Thereafter, he recites the heart-mantra of the tutelary deity of his own family to empower [the disciple] and bestows the initiation; furthermore, he places the aforementioned mudrā upon the crown of the head and upon the neck to bestow the initiation.
Furthermore, the Ācārya again calls out the disciple’s name:
"I now bestow this vidyā upon [Name]; may all the noble deities of the maṇḍala compassionately accept it."
The disciple then proclaims his own aspirations to the worthy and holy ones.

The ācārya again binds the fundamental mudrā of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), consecrates the disciple’s forehead and heart, and bestows empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Furthermore, he binds the four mudrās of the deity of his own family upon the disciple’s head, reciting the mantra once more while conferring empowerment.
The Ācārya says:
"From this day forward, you have fully obtained all the worldly methods of consecration (abhiṣeka).
Furthermore, according to the ritual rules of the vajra-fist, he shall bestow the vajra upon the disciple of consecration, commanding him to hold it constantly."
First, place the vajra bestowed upon the disciple’s heart and confer the empowerment; then place it on the forehead, and next on the crown of the head, conferring the empowerment.
Having conferred the empowerment in this manner, the ācārya says to the disciple: "O noble son!
You have already received empowerment from all the Tathāgatas and all the Vajradharas; you are now preeminent and truly supramundane, as if you had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, the vajra is entrusted to the disciple and they are instructed to uphold it.
The ācārya says: 'You receive this vajra;
you are one who has entered the Vajra-samādhi. This is the supreme vajra that accomplishes all Tathāgatas; by constantly upholding it, you shall attain the supreme wisdom of the vajra.'"
The Vajradhara mantra is: Oṃ sarvatathāgatasiddhi-vajra.
Regarding the secret samaya conferred upon the disciple by the ācārya, one must give rise to a vast and expansive mind and not be stingy or parsimonious.
Why is this? It is because one desires to cause all sentient beings to attain the perfection of great wisdom.
Furthermore, if there are any sentient beings who falsely slander their ācārya, you should protect them.
If there are those who conceive a sense of love and joy for the Dharma, they may be entrusted with the Vajra Secret Samādhi and the seals of the Secret Maṇḍala.
Furthermore, the Ācārya addresses the disciple, saying:
"Possessing the bodhicitta, you shall protect and uphold the secret mind with a resolute will."

"Furthermore, after the disciple has received the various initiations according to their conditions as previously described, they may further be granted the initiation of the Five Buddhas by bestowing that initiation upon them."
Regarding the ritual for empowerment (*abhiṣeka*):

First, one must prepare incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, banners, canopies, and various other articles of offering within the empowerment maṇḍala. Furthermore, no part of the ritual procedures may be lacking; only then should the disciple, having first purified body and mind, be permitted to enter the maṇḍala.

The ācārya performs various ritual acts for the disciple, and then, having bound the mudrā of the *iṣṭadevatā* and recited the mantra of the *iṣṭadevatā*, he confers the initiation (*abhiṣeka*) upon the disciple.
First, for the mudrā of Vairocana Buddha:

extend the two thumbs and the two little fingers apart, while the remaining fingers are all joined together and slightly bent to form the mudrā; place it upon the disciple’s crown and confer the initiation while reciting the mantra of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
The mantra is: "Oṃ sarvatathāgatadharmaiśvara īna sarvatathāgata-vainabhisiñca hūṃ. [Aksobhya Buddha of the East!]
Form the Vajrasattva mudrā:

interlace the two hands to form fists, extend the two middle fingers so they touch like needles to form the seal, and place it upon the disciple’s forehead; then recite the mantra and confer the empowerment.
The mantra is: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatārṇanabhiṣekābhiṣiñca hūṃ*. The seal of the southern Buddha Ratnasaṃbhava:
Using the aforementioned Vajrasattva seal, bend the two middle fingers into the shape of a jewel and place it upon the disciple’s right ear; recite the mantra of the deity and bestow the empowerment.

The mantra is: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatapiṣkaratnanirjāta traṃ*. Regarding the seal of the Western Buddha, Avalokiteśvararāja: using the aforementioned Vajrasattva seal, bend the two middle fingers like lotus petals to form the seal.
Place it behind the crown of the disciple’s head and recite the mantra of the deity while conferring the empowerment.
The mantra is: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatadharmabhiṣekābhiṣiñca hiri*. Regarding the seal of the Buddha Amoghasiddhi of the North:

using the aforementioned Vajrasattva seal, extend the two little fingers and the two middle fingers so that they touch like needles to form the seal. Place it upon the disciple’s left ear, recite the mantra of the deity, and bestow the empowerment.
The mantra is: "Oṃ sarvatathāgataviśvamahāviśvavajrabiñja aḥ. Next, he further bestows the empowerment of the five-buddha crest-garland.

Having thus received the empowerment, it is as if one has been personally conferred the empowerment of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). From this point on, one is entitled to be called a "Great Being" (*mahāpuruṣa*) or an "Ācārya," and receives the most supreme, excellent, and wondrous offerings of the world with sovereign joy.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on the Ācārya. Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Bhagavān, saying: “Bhagavān!

Regarding all the offerings made by an ācārya to the noble deities within the maṇḍala—whether gold, silver, mani-jewels, or any other wealth, even including such gifts as elephants and horses—once the ācārya has received them, what should he do with them?”
"I pray that the Great Muni will explain this for me.
The Buddha said, "Vajrapāṇi!"
The ācārya should possess all items for offering and worship.
Having received them, that ācārya shall divide them into three portions:
the first portion is to be offered to the Triple Gem.
The second portion was given to the brahmins and the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas;
the third portion was further divided into two halves:
one half was given to the ācārya’s fellow students, and the other half was used by the ācārya himself.
Furthermore, the threefold division of the Triple Gem is also divided into three parts:
first, the Buddha; second, the Dharma; and third, the Saṅgha. Having been thus divided, each is to be utilized accordingly.
The portion belonging to the Buddha may be used to fashion images of the Buddha, as well as stupas and temples;
the portion belonging to the Dharma may be used for transcribing all the sutras and teachings of the Tathāgata;
the portion belonging to the Saṃgha may be used to prepare various kinds of food and drink to offer to the assembly of monks.

If the ācārya can thus distinguish the sequence so that they do not mutually infringe upon or damage one another, all the noble deities of every maṇḍala will be fully delighted, and all that is sought shall be accomplished.

If, after the preceptor has divided [the property], someone acting as his steward dwells in a mind of stinginess and misappropriates the property of the Triple Gem, failing to follow the preceptor’s instructions, then due to the law of cause and effect, after his life ends he shall fall into the Raurava Hell. Subsequently, when reborn among humans, he will be born among dogs as a result of his residual karma.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bhagavān, saying:
“The wisdom of all-knowledge is ever present in the minds of all sentient beings; I pray that you will explain for me the practice of all supreme mantras.”
How does a Great Ācārya know the rites of pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), magnetizing (*vaśīkaraṇa*), and subjugation (*abhicāra*)?

Furthermore, how does that Ācārya—who dwells in the wheel of wisdom and extinguishes all sins—[know] the methods for those practitioners who cultivate the corresponding visualizations and the rites of the maṇḍala and homa?
The Buddha said, “Vajrapāṇi!

If an ācārya practices within the mantras, he should possess a heart of great compassion and take pity upon all brāhmaṇas, non-Buddhists, nirgranthas, and others; using words of truth, he should exhort and inspire them, causing them to have faith in the profound and secret Dharma. Furthermore, he should not slander or disparage his fellow students, strictly uphold the five precepts, and practice the profound ten pāramitās to perfect great wisdom.”
Furthermore, the ācārya is able to deliver sentient beings and can grant the eradication of all karmic obstructions;
moreover, he himself abstains from taking life and from false speech, and neither drinks alcohol nor encourages others to do so.
Why is this? Because drinking alcohol is the root of all faults.

Furthermore, if an ācārya acts without sincerity while falsely claiming to possess virtue; or if he is attached to worldly treatises, scripts, and songs; or if he praises the grasping at a self, the grasping at a person, and sentient beings.
“Ācārya, if it is so, you will certainly fall into the miserable realms of hell.
Vajrapāṇi further addressed him, saying:
“If an ācārya practices worldly ways, constantly seeking pleasure, and always consumes wine, meat, and pungent flavors, how can that ācārya lead disciples into the maṇḍala?”
How may disciples be delivered from the perils of saṃsāra?
How may the siddhi of mantras be attained?
I now have doubts as to how these matters are to be understood.
The Buddha said, “Vajrapāṇi! There is no ācārya who,
while practicing the worldly dharmas, constantly seeks pleasure, delights in eating wine, meat, or pungent flavors.”
If there is an ācārya who delights in practicing the yoga of union, he alone is truly entitled to be called an ācārya.
Vajrapāṇi! Listen to the conduct of a bodhisattva; I shall now explain it.

The bodhisattva practitioner upholds the dharma of precepts while practicing the bodhisattva path; with deep faith, firm resolve, and corresponding aspiration, they abide in the non-conceptual and unobstructed dharma. They refrain from false speech, killing, drinking alcohol, frivolous pleasure, and views such as those of self and person. Thus observing the precepts without fault constitutes the bodhisattva conduct practiced by an ācārya.
"If an ācārya is deficient in any matter, he is deficient in wisdom regarding his conduct of the precepts.
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Bhagavān, saying:
"What is called 'wisdom'?"
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! In relation to the three realms, it is called wisdom.”
Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the ‘three realms’?”
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! The mind itself is the triple world.”
Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'mind'?
The Buddha replied:

"The mind is fundamentally devoid of form or characteristics and cannot be grasped or discarded; because it lacks form and characteristics, it pervades all the sense faculties, and by functioning through these faculties, it subsequently becomes attached to objects."
"Just as a monkey encounters a snare, so too is the mind bound by its objects.
Vajrapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How is the triple world described?"
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! The three realms are as follows:”
The realm of greed, the realm of hatred, and the realm of delusion. Vajrapāṇi!
If one is without mind, there is no greed.
If there is no greed, then there is no hatred;
if there is no hatred, then there is no delusion. "Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!
The Bodhisattva’s mind is formless and pervades the six sense faculties; when the faculties and their objects condition one another, attachment arises.

Vajrapāṇi! When the mental activity engages the eye faculty, it perceives what is disagreeable and agreeable; toward the agreeable it gives rise to craving, and toward the disagreeable it gives rise to anger.

Because anger arises in the mind, the darkness of delusion immediately manifests; one is unable to distinguish between what is permissible and what is impermissible, lacks shame and remorse, and feels neither dread nor fear. Due to these causes and conditions, one commits various transgressions; as evil karma blazes forth, one falls into the hells.
Vajrapāṇi! If one is bound by the various fetters of dark karma and the faults of the mental defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion, this is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva Ācārya.

If an ācārya practices the conduct corresponding to that of a bodhisattva, he is as pure and stainless as a crystal gem, his nature is tranquil and his wisdom is perfected, like the moon in the sky, free from all obstruction.

Thereafter, one generates the bodhicitta with firm resolve so that it does not regress; by sealing the sense faculties with the seal of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-mudrā*), one causes those faculties to become subtle and stainless, thereby bringing the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) to full perfection.
Subsequently, one constantly irrigates them with the water of the Dharma-nectar and causes them to grow by fanning them with the wind of sublime liberation. Furthermore...
Abiding in the seal of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-mudrā*) as if the breath were not exhaled, one visualizes a great lotus flower upon one's own heart.
Upon the flower is a full moon disc with white light radiating in the four directions. One further visualizes the seal of samādhi (*samādhi-mudrā*) sealing the center of this.
By means of these seals of samādhi and so forth, one restrains the three karmas (*trikarma*) so they do not become distracted, for even a short period of time.
Remaining silent for a moment, he then awakens [the disciple] by means of mantras and mudrās;
once awakened, he again emits light rays in order to bring the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) to perfection.
The Buddha said:
"The mental image of the moon-disk samādhi-seal, which is the wholesome realm, is precisely the wisdom that is the seed-syllable of the Tathāgata, the Honored One.
Furthermore, the minds of sentient beings abide within the eighteen realms; their bodies are like those lotus flowers, and the flowers possess fragrance."
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!
It is just as when a person perfumes soil or another object with flowers; although the flowers themselves are no longer seen, their fragrance remains. It is exactly like this.

Vajrapāṇi! The seed-syllables of the mantras correspond to that [nature], being like the nature of liberation; until the very end of saṃsāra, the seeds are never severed, and through wisdom and skillful means, they manifest in various forms.

Furthermore, by means of the fragrance of the seed-syllables, the visualization of the ācārya’s body is sustained without ever regressing, enabling the ācārya to embrace all sentient beings and act for their deliverance, even throughout the divisions of day and night without losing the proper time.
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Bhagavān, saying:
“What is meant by ‘time’?
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! At that time, there are two kinds. What are the two?”
The Buddha said:
"First, the internal; second, the external. Vajrapāṇi asked:
"What is meant by 'internal' and 'external'?
The Buddha said, "Vajrapāṇi!"
I shall now explain for you the external time.

As for external time, one day and night is divided into eight great periods (*mahā-kāla*). Two hours constitute one great period; four great periods make one day, and doubling this makes one day and night—these are the eight periods.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!

At the times when the sun and moon rise and set, and when the stars rise and set, these are the times for the practitioner of recitation to perform rites for the pacification of calamities and the increase of prosperity; therein, all one's wishes shall be accomplished.
If, at this time, one generates a mind of diligence and practices for the benefit and happiness of others, no māras or obstacles will dare to approach;
however, if one performs wrathful rites, one should do so at midday or midnight, for if one uses any other time, one will not attain the desired goal.
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
You have already explained the external time; what is the internal time?”
The Buddha said:
“Vajrapāṇi! As for the ‘inner time,’ this refers to that which accords with the supreme teaching of the subtle and secret.”

By means of the wisdom of liberation characterized by the bodhicitta, one explains those mantra-dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, thereby accomplishing the tasks of pacifying, increasing, magnetizing, and subjugating.
During these two periods, one can accomplish two kinds of dharmas, namely:
the dharma of corresponding accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the maṇḍala homa rite.
Just as one obtains this accomplishment like a lapis lazuli gem, which manifests forms and images such that nothing remains hidden, so too are all things accomplished in this very way.
“Vajrapāṇi! Furthermore, one exhausts the remaining time through the five methods of breath:
first, the solar breath; second, the lunar breath; third, the Jvara breath; fourth, the Mūrcchā breath; and fifth, the Subhaga breath.”

First, visualize the sun and moon as two breaths moving within the body, circulating up and down like a lamp illuminating a room; once the darkness has been dispelled and bliss manifests, having thus illuminated [the body], they abide within the abdomen.

Furthermore, one should visualize the third *jāra* breath as a flowing stream of liquid entering the navel center (*nābhi-cakra*), or alternatively, rotating to the left and right; one should further imagine that from the navel center arises a fundamental, birth-giving vajra-lotus, fully blossomed and perfect.
Furthermore, one should visualize the fourth mother, Tārā, like that king’s body—blind and dwelling in darkness within a lotus—yet imagine the royal seal before her.

Furthermore, one visualizes the movement of the breaths of the sun and moon along the left and right sides as well as above and below; the sun abides above and the moon abides below, with the lunar light flowing like waves, pouring forth like nectar.

Fifth is the perception of exquisite fragrance: it descends from the crown of one's head, travels down through the forehead and face to the eyebrows and hairline, reaching the eyes and the nape of the neck, circulating without interruption, abiding in a state of evenness and stability.

"Vajrapāṇi! 'Breath' (śvāsa) is the life-force of sentient beings; 'five' is a conventional designation based on conceptual differentiation. Having employed this to sustain the mind for the duration of that time, or alternatively, having brought to perfect accomplishment the Vajradhātu Lotus-mind for all sentient beings through the method of mantras for the duration of that time, remaining unobstructed and unhindered;

or again, having realized that all sublime dharmas are signless and without utility, and having brought to perfection the bodhicitta of all sentient beings, employing this to abide in the mind for the duration of that time."
"Alternatively, one may complete the excellent maṇḍalas of pacifying, increasing, magnetizing, and subjugating according to their respective times. Vajrapāṇi!
Thus have I now explained these various internal temporal dharmas; you should now practice in accordance with them."
Furthermore, if one relies on such practice at this time, wisdom that gives rise to bliss will naturally abide;
if one delights in wisdom, one will naturally attain the equality of all phenomena;
having attained the equality of phenomena, one attains the stable abiding of the body.
Having attained stability of body, one attains stability of wisdom; through this stabilized wisdom, one knows the dwelling place of the bodhicitta.
Having known the dwelling place of the bodhicitta, one further attains the supreme wisdom of all phenomena; by means of that supreme wisdom, one knows the events of the past, present, and future.
“Vajrapāṇi! Once a bodhisattva has understood that wisdom to have arisen, they must understand the phenomena associated with the visual faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*), namely:
colors such as red and white, and characteristics such as long, short, coarse, and fine.”

Vajrapāṇi! By means of such wisdom-knowledge, the auditory element is generated so that one hears sounds; whatever sounds are heard, they are understood and fully comprehended according to their true meaning and principle.
Vajrapāṇi! In this manner, even such phenomena as the nose, tongue, body, and mind can all be fully exhausted through observation and understanding with the wisdom of wisdom.
"Vajrapāṇi! When an ācārya attains the wisdom of wisdom, he is able to thoroughly understand the supreme meaning of the noble ones;
having understood that supreme meaning of the noble ones, through the skillful means of the wisdom of wisdom and through faith and understanding, he gives rise to the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness)."

Having realized the wisdom of that suchness, one then attains the perfection of all marks and likewise achieves the fulfillment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; through this, the wisdom that knows sentient beings arises.
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva!
Just as I am the Tathāgata within the triple world, possessing the samādhi of the wisdom of all-knowledge and causing all sentient beings to be born into that wisdom, so too does this ācārya.
"Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!

An ācārya and all practitioners who uphold the bodhisattva precepts or the bhikṣu precepts must necessarily distance themselves from the transgression of physical misconduct. Even when engaging in worldly conduct with their own husbands or wives, they should do so as if taking medicine; the wisdom of samādhi thus attained can likewise cause sentient beings to abide in the right path."

That ācārya possesses the samādhis of the three realms; having attained the wisdom that knows the wisdom of sentient beings, he is likewise able to cause the wisdom that knows the wisdom of sentient beings to arise in them as well.
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘sentient beings who are equal through the wisdom of samādhi, wisdom, and skillful means’?”
The Buddha said: “Vajrapāṇi!

When a bodhisattva’s samādhi-wisdom and skillful means are equal to those of sentient beings, it means that these sentient beings are entirely equal and immovable regarding their faculties, the four great elements, and their body, speech, and mind; such sentient beings give rise to that samādhi.”
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!

That wisdom-knowledge of skillful means is most capable of generating the great secret visualization for sentient beings; it is far removed from various signs, and through faith and understanding, one attains the wondrous samādhi of suchness as it truly is, further gaining the realization that one’s own body proceeds upon the right path.
The Buddha said, "Vajrapāṇi!
From my samādhi of the wisdom of the wisdom of the mind of suchness, there are born the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, the Bodhisattva Vajrarāja, the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga, and the Bodhisattva Vajrasādhu."
Furthermore, from the Puṇyaskandha-samādhi, there emerged the Bodhisattvas Vajraratna, Vajraprabha, Vajradhvaja, and Vajrahāsa.
Furthermore, from the samādhi of the gate of wisdom, there emerged the Bodhisattvas Vajradharma, Vajratīkṣṇa, Vajrakāraṇa, and Vajrabhāṣa.
Furthermore, from the Great Vigor Samādhi, there emerged the Bodhisattvas Vajrakarma, Vajrapāla, Vajradaṃṣṭra, and Vajramuṣṭi.
Furthermore, from the samādhi of the joyful mind, there arise the Bodhisattvas Vajralāsyā, Vajramālā, Vajragītā, and Vajranṛtyā.
Furthermore, from the samādhi of perfuming true thusness and so forth, there arise the Bodhisattvas Vajragandha, Vajrapuṣpa, Vajradīpa, and Vajrānulepana.
Furthermore, from the Vajrajñāna-samādhi, there arise the Bodhisattvas Vajrāṅkuśa, Vajrapāśa, Vajrasphoṭa, and Vajraghaṇṭā.

Furthermore, through the transformative manifestations arising from the wisdom-samādhi of the six pāramitās, they bring to perfection the practices for awakening and give birth to the Bodhisattvas Mahāmaitrī, Buddhalocanā, Aparājita, Ūrṇakośa, Śrī-mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī, and Mahāpratisarā.
Furthermore, there were eight world-protecting bodhisattvas who had arisen from the power of great impartial wisdom born of samādhi;

they were: the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.

Furthermore, there is the family of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, which, through countless supernatural powers, manifests as emanated forms of bodhisattvas, the horse-headed Great Vidyārājñī, and devas, humans, asuras, and others, who deliver all sentient beings from great suffering and hardship.

These are: Śvetā Bodhisattvī, Mahāśvetā Bodhisattvī, Māmaki Bodhisattvī, Bhṛkuṭī Bodhisattvī, Khaṇḍarohā Bodhisattvī, Mārīcī Bodhisattvī, Ārya-Cundā Bodhisattvī, Mahāvajrī Bodhisattvī, Ratnamālā Bodhisattvī, Mahāprabhā Bodhisattvī, Jyeṣṭhā Bodhisattvī, and Jyeṣṭhācārī Bodhisattvī.
Furthermore, there is the Vajra Family, which arises from the heart of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; these bodhisattvas, such as the King Vajradhara, are able to bestow accomplishments, namely:
the Bodhisattva Mamaki, the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi, the Bodhisattva Varahi, the Bodhisattva Vajrasphoṭa, the Bodhisattva Vajranr̥tyā, the Bodhisattva Vajragandhari, and the Bodhisattva Vajramekhala.

Furthermore, there were the Bodhisattva Mikhara, the Bodhisattva Vajrakanyā, the Bodhisattva Vajrapaśa, the Bodhisattva Vajrāśu, the Bodhisattva Vajraṭala, the Bodhisattva Vajrajvālāmukha, the Bodhisattva Vajraprabha, the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa, and the Bodhisattva Vajravara-vyūha.
"Furthermore, there are three secrets that give rise to the Great Wrathful Vidyārājas such as Mahābala, Amṛta, and Kuṇḍalī; these Vidyārājas are equal toward the three families."
Furthermore, there are those born from the Vajra-Padma family, or born from samādhi, or born from wisdom, who act as the supreme vidyārājas for rites such as magnetizing and subjugation;
namely, the wrathful vidyārāja Acala, the wrathful vidyārāja Aparājita, and others!
"Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva!
These bodhisattvas, whether through samādhi, wisdom, or skillful means, benefit sentient beings just as the Tathāgata has emerged from the triple world."

“Vajrapāṇi! The Vajra-ācārya, whether a bhikṣu or an upāsaka, should distance himself from the five transgressions, practice the three secrets with faith, and, through samādhi, give rise to wisdom and skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings so that they may develop faith and understanding.”

Furthermore, they enter the great ocean of suffering to rescue and deliver sentient beings; through wisdom and skillful means, they demonstrate the correct path to establish sentient beings therein, ensuring that those beings do not follow deviant paths.

"Vajrapāṇi! Furthermore, if an ācārya acts within the world and delights in practicing worldly ways—engaging in various forms of amusement and consuming the flavors of pungent herbs, wine, and meat—he may practice such worldly ways, yet he cannot be defiled by them."
Why is this? Because that Ācārya has stained his body with wisdom within the three realms, worldly dharmas cannot defile him. Vajrapāṇi!

For example, although sentient beings within the three realms engage in worldly dharmas, they possess various inclinations and, by relying on samādhi, are able to bring benefit to all sentient beings within the world.
"Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!
One who is not an ācārya, nor one who practices and maintains the precepts, nor one who practices the yoga, cannot cause sentient beings to abide in unsurpassed wisdom."
Vajrapāṇi said: “So it is, so it is.
An ācārya who practices and maintains the precepts shall attain unsurpassed wisdom.”

“Vajrapāṇi! Regarding the Dharma of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, even if a bhikṣu were to exert great diligence in its practice, he would not be able to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) for himself, let alone cause other sentient beings to attain unsurpassed enlightenment.”
The Buddha said, “Vajrapāṇi!
It is as if there were someone, or even mosquitoes and gadflies, who, exhausting all their strength, were to strike Mount Sumeru with their hands and feet; they could never cause it any damage.”
Vajrapāṇi! A bhikṣu who practices according to the prātimokṣa precepts will ultimately never attain unsurpassed wisdom.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!

If there be a bhikṣu or a layperson who, by practicing the secret teachings as an ācārya, is able to cause all sentient beings to produce the seeds of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās respect, revere, and make offerings to them?
"Vajrapāṇi! Just as I, the Tathāgata, abide within the triple world, so shall you make offerings.
